metadata.title: Color Never Hears the Music: Why a Fast Tune Gets a Yellow Sky
metadata.note: words come from the signed script; figures on screen are read from committed files or the cited paper, never typed

beats.title: THE QUESTION
beats.narration_text: Two skies, one yellow and one blue-grey. Two bits of music, one quick and bright, one slow and low. Which sky goes with which?
beats.on_screen: headline "Which sky goes with which?" from frame one over a grey sky. Clouds drift fast under the quick tune (label "A: quick, bright"), then slowly under the slow tune (label "B: slow, low"). Then two swatches appear at the lower edge of the sky, "1 yellow" and "2 blue-grey", in an order that does not match the order played.
beats.source_on_screen: "Illustration: our tunes, our skies. Not data."

beats.title: MOST PEOPLE AGREE
beats.narration_text: I'm Tanmay Kulkarni, for Humanitarians AI. If you put yellow on the quick one, you chose the way most listeners do.
beats.on_screen: headline "Most listeners pick yellow for quick". The sky warms to yellow while the quick tune returns; a small ring marks the matched pair. A name line fades in inside the safe area ("Tanmay Kulkarni · Humanitarians AI").
beats.source_on_screen: "Palmer et al., PNAS 2013: US and Mexico."

beats.title: THE STUDY
beats.narration_text: Researchers at Berkeley tested this with real music by Bach, Mozart and Brahms. About ninety seven people, in the United States and in Mexico, picked colors for each piece. Quick, major music drew lighter, yellower colors. Slow, minor music drew darker, bluer ones.
beats.on_screen: headline "A real test, two countries". Labels appear in order: "Bach · Mozart · Brahms", "97 listeners · US + Mexico", "picked colors for each piece". Then "quick + major → lighter, yellower" while the sky is yellow; the tune slows and the sky cools to blue-grey as "slow + minor → darker, bluer" appears.

beats.title: THE GO-BETWEEN
beats.narration_text: But a sky doesn't sound like anything, so they must be matching feeling. Listeners rated the music, and the colors, as happy or sad, strong or weak, and the two sets of ratings lined up very closely.
beats.on_screen: headline "They match through feeling". The strip comes up (HAPPY–SAD across, STRONG–WEAK up). A music dot and a color dot slide in one after the other and land on the same spot. A small line reads "ratings of music vs. colors: up to 0.99".
beats.source_on_screen: "Emotion ratings, music vs. chosen colors: 0.89–0.99 (Palmer et al. 2013). Correlation, not proof."

beats.title: THEIR OWN EXAMPLE
beats.narration_text: The paper gives its own example. Bach's fast dance feels happy and energetic, and fits a saturated yellow. Brahms's slow Adagio feels sad, and fits a dark grey.
beats.on_screen: headline "Their own example". The dots move to the HAPPY end: label "Bach · fast dance" and a saturated-yellow swatch lands beside the dots; the sky is yellow. Then the dots move to the SAD end: label "Brahms · slow Adagio", a dark-grey swatch lands; the sky cools.
beats.source_on_screen: "The paper's own example of its idea (Palmer et al. 2013)."

beats.title: THE SWAP
beats.narration_text: Now swap them, and a quick tune under a blue-grey sky feels wrong, because the two feelings no longer agree.
beats.on_screen: headline "Swap them and it clashes". The quick tune plays over the blue-grey sky; the two dots split apart and the gap is labelled "disagree", pulsing once.

beats.title: THE LIMIT
beats.narration_text: One limit is that this is a correlation, and the test used only two countries and Western classical music.
beats.on_screen: headline "Strong, not a law". A three-line label stack appears one line at a time: "correlation", "2 countries", "Western classical only". The sky drifts slowly warmer.
beats.source_on_screen: "Palmer et al. 2013: unclear for non-Western scales."

beats.title: TRY IT
beats.narration_text: To test it yourself, try the quick, minor case. It's in the full film: "Color Never Hears the Music: Why a Fast Tune Gets a Yellow Sky".
beats.on_screen: headline "Test your own". The sky returns to yellow with the quick tune (the opening state). The closing card (the exact film title and "Humanitarians AI", inside the safe area) comes in on the spoken word "Color" and stays about 4.4 s; in the final 1.0 s it fades out as the sky eases back to the opening grey (as built and measured; the first plan said about 3 s and 0.7 s).
beats.source_on_screen: "Palmer et al. tested US and Mexico only."
